newsitem.title: JAPAN: Dollar rises sharply on Japan official's remarks.
newsitem.headline: Dollar rises sharply on Japan official's remarks.

text.p: The dollar skyrocketed on Thursday after an influential Japanese official said that the nation's trade surplus was not a cause for concern.

The dollar surged to 115.80 yen by early afternoon, a steep 4.5 yen jump from Wednesday's New York close, after the remarks by Eisuke Sakakibara, head of the Ministry of Finance's International Finance Bureau.
By late Tokyo trading the dollar was quoted at 114.40 yen.
The dollar's rise also helped push up Tokyo shares since a weaker Japanese currency helps exporters. The Nikkei 225-share average closed with a gain of 1.35 percent at 20,564.46.

Sakakibara said that Japan's trade surplus will not be a major issue at the June 20-22 summit meeting of the Group of Seven (G7) industrialised nations in Denver and that a drastic expansion in Japan's current account surplus will not happen.
The yen has been rising against the dollar since early May amid growing fears that a rebound in Japan's trade surplus could revive trade friction with the United States.
"A drastic expansion of the surplus cannot happen," Sakakibara told reporters after giving a speech at a financial seminar in Tokyo.
"I think the issue (Japan's surplus) is being played up excessively," he added.

The government said on Wednesday that the surplus in the current account, the broadest measure of trade in goods and services, rose 92.7 percent from a year ago to 1.09 trillion yen ($9.56 billion) in April.
A strong yen makes Japanese products more expensive abroad and should in theory reduce the trade surplus.
Sakakibara later told reporters that the Japanese government was resolved to prevent any excessive swings in foreign exchange markets.
"The prime minister has instructed us to act against forex moves in a timely and appropriate manner. We will act decisively against excessive forex moves," he said.

The dollar also received a boost from comments by Tomomitsu Oba, the former vice finance minister for international affairs, who said that Sakakibara has in mind a yen rate slightly stronger than 120 yen to the dollar, currency traders said.
Oba made the remarks to reporters after he and Sakakibara spoke at a private economic seminar.
Sakakibara also said Japan's interest rates, which are currently standing at record low levels, are unlikely to rise anytime soon, according to participants in the seminar.

However, the dollar later reversed course and fell two yen from its peak on speculation the U.S. Big Three automakers might call for a stronger yen when they meet U.S. President Bill Clinton on June 27.

White House spokesman Mike McCurry said on Wednesday that Clinton and the Big Three auto executives will meet on June 27 and discuss the impact on the auto industry of U.S.-Japan agreements to increase U.S.-made automobile and auto part exports to Japan.
Douglas Herberger, president of General Motors Japan Ltd, said that he sees a dollar/yen exchange rate of between 95-105 yen as appropriate.
